snapshot.title: SSC History: Medieval India — Sultanate & Mughals
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ SSC History Hook: Slave: Aibak. Khilji: Market. Panipat 1: 1526. Akbar: Sikri/Jizya. Shah Jahan: Taj. Aurangzeb: Zinda Pir.

quick_notes.title: Delhi Sultanate (5 Dynasties)
quick_notes.detail: Slave (Qutubuddin Aibak), Khilji (Alauddin - Market reforms), Tughlaq (M.B. Tughlaq - token currency), Sayyid, Lodi (Ibrahim - lost 1st Panipat 1526).
quick_notes.explanation: The Delhi Sultanate was a series of five Muslim dynasties that ruled from Delhi, starting around 1206 and ending in 1526. The Slave dynasty, named because its first ruler Qutubuddin Aibak was originally a slave soldier, began the Sultanate. The Khilji dynasty is known for Alauddin Khilji, who introduced market reforms to control prices of goods like grain and cloth. The Tughlaq dynasty's Muhammad bin Tughlaq attempted a token currency, meaning he replaced silver coins with cheap copper and brass ones that people could use as money, but the plan failed because they were too easy to counterfeit. The Sayyid dynasty followed, and then the Lodi dynasty, whose last ruler Ibrahim Lodi lost the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, ending the Sultanate.

quick_notes.title: Alauddin Khilji
quick_notes.detail: Introduced "Dagh" (branding of horses) and "Chehra" (descriptive roll of soldiers). Market control and price regulation.
quick_notes.explanation: Alauddin Khilji was a Sultan of Delhi who ruled from 1296 to 1316. To prevent cheating in his army, he introduced a system called Dagh, which meant branding each horse with a hot iron mark to ensure soldiers did not swap or sell royal horses. He also created the Chehra system, which was a written descriptive roll of every soldier's face and appearance, so the army could track each man and stop fake soldiers from collecting extra pay. To keep his empire stable and his soldiers paid, Alauddin set strict market control, meaning the government fixed the prices of all goods like food, cloth, and weapons. He also enforced price regulation, which meant shopkeepers could not charge more than the set price, and if they cheated, they were severely punished.

quick_notes.title: The Mughal Empire (1526–1857)
quick_notes.detail: Babur (Founder), Humayun, Akbar (Greatest, Din-i-Ilahi), Jahangir (Chain of Justice), Shah Jahan (Golden age of Architecture), Aurangzeb (Alamgir).
quick_notes.explanation: The Mughal Empire ruled much of India from 1526 to 1857. It was founded by Babur, who won the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. His son Humayun briefly lost the empire but later regained it. The greatest Mughal ruler was Akbar, who created a new religion called Din-i-Ilahi, meaning "Divine Faith," to unite his diverse subjects. Akbar's son Jahangir became famous for his "Chain of Justice," a literal gold chain outside his palace that anyone could ring to get a direct hearing from the emperor. Shah Jahan, Jahangir's son, is known for the Golden Age of Architecture, during which he built the Taj Mahal. The last great Mughal emperor was Aurangzeb, who took the title Alamgir, meaning "Conqueror of the World," and expanded the empire to its largest size.

quick_notes.title: Akbar's Reforms
quick_notes.detail: Abolished Jizya. Introduced Mansabdari system. Built Fatehpur Sikri and Ibadat Khana.
quick_notes.explanation: Akbar, a Mughal emperor, abolished Jizya, which was a special tax that non-Muslims had to pay in an Islamic state. He introduced the Mansabdari system, a ranking system for military officers and administrators where each official, called a mansabdar, was assigned a rank that determined his salary and the number of soldiers he had to provide. He also built the city of Fatehpur Sikri, which served as his capital, and within it he constructed the Ibadat Khana, a house of worship where scholars from different religions could debate and discuss ideas.

quick_notes.title: Monuments
quick_notes.detail: Qutub Minar (Aibak/Iltutmish). Red Fort & Taj Mahal (Shah Jahan). Buland Darwaza (Akbar).
quick_notes.explanation: Monuments are large, historically important buildings or structures that are protected by law. The Qutub Minar in Delhi was started by Qutb-ud-din Aibak, a ruler of the Slave Dynasty, and finished by his successor Iltutmish. The Red Fort and the Taj Mahal, both in Agra, were built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. The Buland Darwaza, a massive gateway, was built at Fatehpur Sikri by the Mughal emperor Akbar to celebrate his victory over Gujarat. Each of these monuments is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which means it is recognized internationally as having outstanding value to all of humanity.

lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Age of Empires'. Medieval history in SSC is dominated by the 'Delhi Sultanate' and the 'Mughals'. Questions focus on 'Rulers', 'Monuments', and 'Administration'. From the Qutub Minar to the Taj Mahal and the reforms of Akbar—these are the markers of our history. Do you know who started the 'Sijda' system? Or which Mughal king was called 'Zinda Pir'? Let's master the medieval timeline today.
